I’ve been farming this wheat-maize rotation on my 5 mu plot for 15 years now, so I know what works around here. With six people in the house and some of the family working off-farm, I don’t have endless labor to spare, but I do have a reliable well, so water is not my biggest worry.

For wheat, I’ll plant the whole 5 mu this autumn with an improved variety—Jimai 22 or something similar—because the improved seeds give stable yields and resist lodging better than the old traditional types. Before sowing I’ll run the rotary tiller once to break up the stubble and level the field. I’ll put down a basal compound fertilizer and then top-dress with urea at green-up and jointing. In total that comes to about 15 kg of nitrogen, 5 kg of phosphorus, and 2 kg of potassium per mu. Irrigation is key for wheat on the North China Plain: I’ll water four times—before winter, at returning-green, at jointing, and once more at grain filling. Weeds and aphids are the usual problems, so I plan three pesticide applications: one herbicide and two sprayings for insects/fungus. If the weather cooperates I expect about 1,100 kg per mu.

For maize, timing is everything because the summer window between wheat harvest and maize harvest is short. I’ve learned that no-tillage direct seeding right after cutting the wheat saves me precious days and labor, so I’ll skip ploughing for the maize. I’ll sow a hybrid like Denghai 605 on the same 5 mu because those hybrids yield well and stand up to the summer storms. Maize needs plenty of nitrogen, so I’ll apply around 18 kg N per mu together with about 5 kg P and 4 kg K, mostly at sowing and a side-dress at the big-flare stage. With the well I can irrigate twice—once when the plants are knee-high and again at silking. Weeds and corn borers are the main threats, so two pesticide rounds (one herbicide, one insecticide) should be enough. A good year should give me roughly 1,150 kg per mu.
